newsitem.title: USA: Mexico bank woes will take time to resolve - Ortiz.
newsitem.headline: Mexico bank woes will take time to resolve - Ortiz.

text.p: Mexico has not yet entirely solved its banking sector woes but it is working toward that end, Finance Secretary Guillermo Ortiz said Wednesday.
"Certainly, this is not a solved problem; this is a problem that will take some time to consolidate," Ortiz told a news conference at the Mexican Embassy.
The Mexican government has estimated that it will have to spend the equivalent of eight percent of its GDP to clean up the debris of the 1995 banking crisis.
The fragility of national banking systems has become a hot button topic in the joint annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank being held in Washington.

Both IMF managing director Michel Camdesus and World Bank president James Wolfensohn have urged member countries to beef up their banking regulations and surveillance systems in order to avoid a crash like the one Mexico suffered last year.
Ortiz noted that other countries, particularly in Latin America and Scandinavia, had suffered banking crises and that now there was concern about some Asian nations.
The Mexican government has taken steps to restructure and strengthen its banking system, including setting up the FOBAPROA fund to buy bad loans from troubled banks.
Ortiz said that in the next few weeks Mexico would decide how much of the 100 billion pesos FOBAPROA has accumulated in bad loans will be sold to spawn a market for troubled debt.

In answer to a question about protests staged by bank and credit card debtors, who were stung by last year's devaluation and the spike in domestic interest rates, Ortiz said that the government was trying to ease their burden.
"The government is concerned about the over-indebtedness of families and businesses," he said. "But it is evident that we can't solve everybody's problems overnight".
